question: Over oceans and remote areas without radar or VHF, what kind of control does ATC usually provide?

options.text: No control service of any kind

explanation: Without radar or VHF, ATC provides a procedural service, generally on HF. This needs large vertical, lateral and longitudinal separations, so traffic density is low.

question: Why does procedural control over the oceans limit traffic density?

options.text: It allows only one aircraft per flight level per day
It does not permit any change of level
It requires every aircraft to carry two HF sets
It needs large separations between aircraft

explanation: Position reports are infrequent and less accurate, so large separations are required, which limits how many aircraft can use the airspace.

question: Crossing the North Atlantic, how often are position reports made south of 70°N?
explanation: Reports are made every 10° of longitude up to 70°N and every 20° north of that, giving ATC a position update roughly every 30–60 minutes.

question: North of 70°N on the North Atlantic, how often are position reports made?

options.text: Only at the oceanic exit point

explanation: North of 70°N the meridians are closer together, so reports are made every 20° of longitude instead of every 10°.

question: With ocean reporting points, how often does ATC typically receive a position update?
explanation: Reporting every 10° (or 20°) of longitude gives ATC a position update about every 30 to 60 minutes, which is a major limitation as traffic grows.

question: In remote areas on HF, how does the pilot usually exchange messages with the controller?

options.text: Directly, on a dedicated HF frequency
By VHF relay through another aircraft only
Through a third party who relays them

explanation: Because HF is difficult to use, the pilot rarely talks directly to the controller; a radio operator relays the messages between them.

question: What position accuracy does global satellite navigation now give?
explanation: GNSS gives position accuracy better than one nautical mile almost globally, which is what makes reduced separation possible.

question: Until the late 1980s, how did aircraft communicate with ATC and operators?

options.text: By VHF and HF voice only

explanation: Until the late 1980s communications were only by VHF and HF voice. Data link and satellite communications came later.

question: Why is VHF limited to areas near habitable land?

options.text: It is absorbed by the sea surface beyond the coast
It is reflected by the ionosphere
It is line of sight, from ground stations
It cannot be used above FL300

explanation: VHF travels by line of sight, so it is only available over and near the land where its ground stations are.

question: What is the approximate VHF range from a ground transmitter for an aircraft at FL300?
explanation: The line-of-sight range for an aircraft at FL300 is about 200 NM, roughly 1.23 × √30 000 ≈ 213 NM.

question: What are the main problems of HF communication?

options.text: Static interference and fading of the signal
Line-of-sight range and the very high power needed

explanation: HF suffers high levels of static interference and fading, so messages are often repeated or relayed through other aircraft.

question: Why does the pilot not keep a continuous listening watch on HF?

options.text: HF is only switched on at the reporting points on the route
A SELCAL system alerts the crew when there is a message
HF messages are only sent as text
The autopilot listens for the crew

explanation: Listening to noisy HF is stressful, so a selective calling system, SELCAL, is activated by the ground operator to alert the crew when there is a message for them.

question: In the 1990s, voice communication was extended through which satellites?

options.text: Low polar orbit satellites, using HF

explanation: SATCOM voice was introduced in the 1990s through geostationary satellites, using UHF frequencies.

question: Why is geostationary SATCOM coverage limited to about 80° of latitude?

options.text: Geostationary satellites can only be above the equator
The polar ice reflects the signal
The aircraft antenna points only upwards
The satellites switch off when they pass over the poles

explanation: Geostationary satellites sit over the equator, so they are low on the horizon, and then out of sight, near the poles. Coverage reaches only about 80° of latitude.

question: How is SATCOM to be provided in polar regions?

options.text: By a network of VHF ground stations on the polar ice
By satellites in lower, inclined orbits

explanation: Satellites in lower altitude orbits, inclined so that they pass over the polar regions, are intended to give a full SATCOM service there.

question: What is ACARS?

options.text: A system that records the cockpit voices for the operator to review
A voice system for HF communication
A data link for messages between aircraft and ATC or operators

explanation: The aircraft communication addressing and reporting system passes messages by data link between the aircraft and ATC or the operator. Messages can be printed in the cockpit.

question: Which medium did ACARS first use?
explanation: ACARS first used VHF. In the early 1990s it was extended to SATCOM for flights outside VHF coverage.

question: How was the polar gap in ACARS coverage closed in 2001?

options.text: By extending the service to HF
By adding VHF stations in the Arctic
By relaying messages through other aircraft

explanation: Geostationary SATCOM does not reach the poles, so in 2001 the gap was closed by extending ACARS to HF data link.

question: What did the 1990s interface between ACARS and the FMS allow?

options.text: The FMS to be loaded with a new navigation database while in flight
The crew to talk to ATC by voice through the FMS
ATC to fly the aircraft remotely
Weather and alternate routes to be evaluated in the FMS

explanation: Operational data, such as weather and alternate flight plan routes, could be sent to the FMS and evaluated there. Maintenance monitoring functions were also added.

question: Through which units is data link implemented on the flight deck?
explanation: Data link is implemented through the ATSU (air traffic service unit) and the DCDU (data link cockpit display unit).

question: How is the pilot alerted to an incoming data link message?

options.text: By visual and aural attention getters
By a message shown on the standby compass display
By a call from the cabin crew

explanation: Lights and sounds, the attention getters, alert the pilot to a new data link message. A printer gives a hard copy.

question: Which of these services can an ATSU provide?

options.text: Load sheets and passenger lists for the operator only

explanation: An ATSU provides flight information, alerting, air traffic advisory and air traffic control services (area, approach and aerodrome).

question: What is CNS/ATM designed to give?

options.text: A seamless global air traffic management system
A complete replacement for all onboard navigation equipment
A global network of primary radars

explanation: CNS/ATM uses automation, digital technology and satellite systems to create a seamless global air traffic management system.

question: In CNS/ATM, what does "air traffic management" refer to?

options.text: The navigation equipment carried on board the aircraft
The radar coverage of a state
The facilities of the aircraft operational centre

explanation: Communications, navigation and surveillance refer to the facilities of an ATSU; air traffic management refers to those of the aircraft operational centre, basically the airline.

question: What is an AOC in this context?

options.text: The airline or company operating the aircraft
The aerodrome operating committee at each airport

explanation: The aircraft (or airline) operational centre is basically the airline or company operating the aircraft.

question: Which of these is an ATM data link message?
explanation: ATM messages exchanged with an ATSU include departure clearances, oceanic clearances and digital ATIS. Load sheets, passenger information and maintenance reports are AOC messages.

question: What is D-ATIS?

options.text: ATIS read by a synthetic voice
ATIS sent only to aircraft on the ground
Terminal information sent by data link
ATIS broadcast on a second VHF frequency

explanation: Data link ATIS delivers the automatic terminal information service as a text message instead of a voice broadcast.

question: What does OOOI stand for in AOC messages?

options.text: Out of gate, off ground, on ground, in gate
Oceanic, overland, outbound and inbound sectors
On time, off time, overdue, in time

explanation: OOOI messages report Out of the gate, Off the ground, On the ground and In the gate, so the operator knows where its aircraft are.

question: Why does the operator want OOOI and other AOC messages?

options.text: To meet the ATC clearance requirements
To replace the flight data recorder
To know where its aircraft are, for efficient operation
To give ATC the aircraft's exact position for separation purposes

explanation: The airline needs to know where its aircraft are at all times for efficient, cost-effective operation, so a data link passes progress and other messages.

question: Which of these is an AOC data link message?
explanation: AOC messages include OOOI, load sheets, passenger information, weather reports, maintenance reports and free text. Clearances are ATM messages.

question: How does the pilot start a data link session with an ATSU?

options.text: By a manual logon with the ATSU's four-letter address
By selecting SELCAL to the ATSU code
Automatically, when the engines are started at the gate
By calling the ATSU on VHF voice

explanation: The pilot enters the four-letter address of the ATSU into the FMS, which sends the logon message. The logon includes the aircraft address and the services it supports.

question: What is the logon and connection process called?

options.text: The controller pilot data link, CPDLC

explanation: Logon, acknowledgement, connection request and connection confirm together form the ATS facilities notification, AFN.

question: After the ATSU acknowledges a logon, what does it send?
explanation: The ATSU acknowledges the logon and sends a connection request; the aircraft replies with a connection confirm, completing the process.

question: When must the initial manual logon be made?

options.text: Only on the ground before departure, and never again in flight
At first contact, entering CPDLC airspace, or after a break

explanation: Logon is made on first contact with the ATSU on the ground, when entering a CPDLC area from a non-CPDLC area, and after any interruption of the service.

question: Once data link service is established, how is the aircraft passed to the next CPDLC unit?

options.text: By a new manual logon each time

explanation: After the service is established, the equipment transfers automatically to subsequent CPDLC-capable ATSUs.

question: A message sent from an aircraft on the ground to the ATSU is called:
explanation: Messages from the aircraft to the ATSU are always downlinks and from the ATSU to the aircraft uplinks, even when the aircraft is on the ground.

question: What is the aim of FANS?

options.text: Replacing the FMS with ground computers
Providing radar cover over all oceans
Integrated ATC without radar, using GNSS and data link
Replacing every ILS with satellite approaches at all airports

explanation: FANS uses GNSS for position and data link and voice via satellites to give ATC continuous position information and direct pilot-controller communication where radar is unavailable.

question: What will FANS allow ATC to do with separation?

options.text: Remove it entirely in oceanic airspace
Keep it the same, with fewer reports
Increase it to allow for errors

explanation: Continuous, accurate positions and direct communication allow separation distances to be significantly reduced.

question: If FANS position accuracy is degraded, what still protects aircraft from conflicts?
explanation: If position accuracy is degraded for any reason, aircraft still have TCAS to warn of any potential conflict.

question: In which airspace is FANS A used?

options.text: High density airspace with good VHF

explanation: FANS A serves oceanic and remote airspace, transmitted over the ACARS network. FANS B serves high density airspace with good VHF coverage.

question: What does FANS A provide?

options.text: Primary radar coverage and VHF voice communication only

explanation: FANS A provides a communications, navigation and surveillance system and automatic dependent surveillance (ADS), with GNSS supplying the navigation.

question: Over which network is FANS A transmitted?
explanation: FANS A is transmitted over the ACARS network. FANS B uses the aeronautical telecommunications network, ATN.

question: How do some operators use FANS A in all phases of flight?

options.text: To monitor gate departure, take-off, landing and gate arrival
To carry out automatic landings in low visibility conditions
To file flight plans with ATC

explanation: Some operators use FANS A to monitor aircraft progress: gate departure, take-off, landing and arrival, plus in-flight progress and system operation.

question: Which combination of services may an ATSU not use together?
explanation: An ATSU may use AFN, ADS or CPDLC alone, or AFN with CPDLC, or ADS with CPDLC, but not AFN with ADS.

question: In which airspace does FANS B operate?

options.text: Polar regions without any satellite coverage
High density airspace with good VHF coverage

explanation: FANS B is very similar to FANS A but operates in high density airspace with good VHF coverage, over the ATN.

question: What is the aeronautical telecommunications network?

options.text: A network linking ground, air and avionic data subnetworks
A network of VHF voice stations
A worldwide network of HF stations used for SELCAL calls

explanation: The ATN is an internetwork architecture that lets ground-ground, ground-air and avionics data subnetworks inter-operate.

question: What does CPDLC stand for?

options.text: Communication protocol for digital data link messages

explanation: CPDLC lets the controller and pilot exchange clearances and requests as text messages by data link.

question: What does ADS-C stand for?
explanation: In ADS-C the ground system sets up a contract with the aircraft to report its position automatically at set times or events.

question: Which frequency range is HF?
explanation: HF is 3–30 MHz. VHF is 30–300 MHz and MF is 300 kHz–3 MHz.

question: Which frequency range is VHF?
explanation: VHF is defined as 30–300 MHz. Aircraft VHF communication uses part of it, around 118–137 MHz.
